ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Meconium aspiration: 4

A newborn with severe meconium aspiration has profound hypoxemia and echocardiographic evidence of high pulmonary vascular resistance with right-to-left shunting. Which associated physiological disorder explains the additional impairment of systemic oxygenation in this infant?

  1. Prioritize effective ventilation; suction only when obstruction warrants it
  2. Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
  3. Meconium aspiration syndrome
  4. Partial airway obstruction with air trapping
  5. Chemical pneumonitis with surfactant dysfunction
Answer and explanation

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

Persistently high pulmonary vascular resistance can drive right-to-left shunting and worsen hypoxemia in severe neonatal lung disease.

Option explanations

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn: Persistently high pulmonary vascular resistance can drive right-to-left shunting and worsen hypoxemia in severe neonatal lung disease.

Meconium aspiration syndrome: Respiratory distress after meconium exposure in a term or post-term infant can reflect aspiration-related lung disease; other causes still require consideration. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Partial airway obstruction with air trapping: A ball-valve effect permits inspiration more readily than expiration, promoting hyperinflation and air leak. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Chemical pneumonitis with surfactant dysfunction: Meconium injures the lung and disrupts surfactant, contributing to impaired gas exchange and atelectasis. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Prioritize effective ventilation; suction only when obstruction warrants it: Routine suction solely for meconium exposure can delay needed ventilation. Obstruction preventing effective ventilation may require airway clearance. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
